message.reasoning:
I'm planning a JUnit 4 test suite for CommandLine, using the package-private constructor and addArg/addOption since the tests live in the same package. I'll need to construct Option instances to populate values for testing the various getter methods like getOptionValue, getOptionValues, and hasOption.

Since it's the actual compiled Option class from this commons-cli revision, I'm recalling its real API: constructors taking opt/description, opt/hasArg/description, and opt/longOpt/hasArg/description, plus methods like getOpt, setLongOpt, hasArg, getValue, getValuesList, setRequired, setType, setValueSeparator, and clone. I'm trying to remember whether addValue is package-private or public in this version.

Since addArg and addOption on CommandLine are package-private and CommandLine's constructor is also package-private with no args, I can write the test in the same package to access everything directly. I'm planning test methods: checking hasOption by short name and by char, getOptionValue as a string and as a char, and getOptionValue with a default value for both string and char cases.

Adding more test methods now: handling multiple values via getOptionValues, type-converted values via getOptionObject using TypeHandler, retrieving args and arg lists, getOptions, iterating options, resolving long option names, confirming null is returned when an option isn't set, handling hyphen-stripped option names, and verifying getOptionObject returns null when unset. I'm also checking whether Option's addValue method is accessible from the same package so I can set multiple values on an option.

I'm recalling the Option class fields and constructor signature from the commons-cli 1.1 source to make sure I'm instantiating options correctly in these tests.

There's also value-related methods like setValueSeparator, addValue (deprecated), processValue, and accessors for getting values. I'm thinking addValue is fine to use since it's a deprecated but still functional public method that just delegates to processValue.

Since the test class lives in the same package as Option, I can call addValue directly without reflection, even if it's package-private, since Java allows same-package access without needing a subclass relationship.

Now I'm checking how resolveOption strips leading hyphens from the opt parameter before comparing it against the option's short or long name.

I also want to verify edge cases like getOptionValues returning null for unset options, and double-check TypeHandler.createValue's behavior for a plain String type to confirm it just returns the input unless there's a parsing error.

So for a String-type option, getOptionObject should just return the same value as getOptionValue. Now I'll plan out roughly 20 test cases, setting up a helper method to build an Option with a single value, and starting with basic hasOption tests to confirm options are recognized correctly after being added to a CommandLine.

Next I want to verify hasOption works with the char overload the same way as the String version, then check that leading hyphens get stripped properly when checking option names -- I need to confirm whether Util.stripLeadingHyphens handles one or two hyphens correctly.

For the long option name test, I'm setting up a case where an Option has both a short name "a" and long name "alpha", then checking that hasOption recognizes both forms.

Then I'm drafting more test cases: retrieving the first value when an option has multiple values added, verifying the char overload works the same way, confirming getOptionValue returns null for missing options, and checking that the default-value overload falls back correctly when the option isn't set.
